rv.q: Ecstatic catharsis is her métier, and Animal Wisdom is luminous with it.
Heather Christian has created one of the most unclassifiable works in contemporary American theater, and also one of the most profound.
At that point, a choir of several dozen singers enters and the music takes over, swallowing the room with a sense of communal reverie.
Animal Wisdom will take you farther than you’ve been before, and you won’t even be in a church.
And when someone writes music this soul-stirring, you ought to believe they know a thing or two about souls.
After a while, the assemblage of cursory remembrances, divine allusions, and supernatural digressions becomes fatiguing.
If you don’t expect more, you won’t be disappointed.
But “Animal Wisdom” struck me as largely busy, distracting and diffuse.
Animal Wisdom ends up offering a hard-to-comprehension meditation on mourning that feels more for herself than for us.

Following an admittedly stunning staging coup, the lengthy climactic sequence (somewhere between twenty and thirty minutes) is played out in darkness relieved only occasionally by a nanosecond's flash of light. I have rarely felt more held hostage in a theatre.
Heather Christian's folk-blues requiem is the most unclassifiable—and one of the most unforgettable—shows in New York right now.
There’s a muchness to Animal Wisdom that is both admirable and daunting.

The show asks audiences to participate in what Christian insists is “real” ritual—complete with Coca-Cola communion, bell-ringing, and extended periods of total darkness—but delivers neither the catharsis of meaningful drama nor the comfort of genuine spiritual practice. The production’s fundamental flaw is Nick Kourtides’ sound design.

Christian is not interested in narrative clarity nearly as much as emotional excavation, channeling the strange spaces where loss, ancestry, spirituality, madness, music, and longing begin to blur together.
Thrillingly, the music and lyrical poetry bring together tropes about life and death and communing with ancestral spirits to heal.

cn.t: Critics find Christian's genre-defying musical autobiography visceral and original but divisive. While some praise its spiritual power and Miller's performance as transformative, others find it vague and overstuffed, struggling under its ambitious conceptual weight.
